slides.title: Flow Control
slides.say: Welcome. This chapter teaches how a program decides. Every concept has an idea, an everyday picture, a drawn mechanism, the code and what the run printed. The same examples run on the chapter page, in the same order.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Five parts, each a run of slides you can jump to. Every code example sits in the chapter-code tab of the page in this same order. Example: part three has five examples about blocks and branches. Ask the class: which part do you expect to be hardest, and why?

slides.title: Two questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Two questions guide the chapter. How does a program choose what to do, and what makes a condition true? What does current Python add to the book? Example: the match statement. Ask the class to guess the answer to the first question now.

slides.title: Part 1: Booleans and comparisons
slides.say: Part one. A Boolean value is the answer to a yes or no question, and comparison operators ask the questions. Predict each result before the run. Example: is seven below nine? Ask the class which comparison surprises them.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: values and comparisons
slides.say: A switch is on or off, like a Boolean value, and scales compare two things. Read each row aloud and let the class add a picture of their own. Example: the height bar at a fairground. Ask: which picture fits greater than or equal to?

slides.title: Boolean values: only two answers
slides.say: A Boolean value is the answer to a yes or no question, and Python has exactly two of them. Example: a light switch is on or off. Ask the class: why is it handy that True also counts as the number one?

slides.title: Boolean values: True and False
slides.say: Read the three results on the slide. True plus True is two, because the values are numbers in disguise. The bool function turns zero into False and everything else into True. Ask the class to predict bool of minus three and a half.

slides.title: Comparison operators: six questions
slides.say: Six operators ask six questions, and each one answers True or False. Example: is seven below nine? Ask the class: what is the difference between the single equals sign and the double equals sign? Draw the four steps on the board, then compare them with the slide.

slides.title: Comparison operators
slides.say: The table shows the six questions about x and y with their answers. Notice that the not-equal operator is the exact opposite of the equal operator. Ask the class to change y to seven and predict the new row of answers.

slides.title: Equality: what counts as the same
slides.say: Equality needs the same kind of value. A number never equals a string, and a capital letter is a different character. Example: 42 and the text 42. Ask the class: why would anyone compare text typed by a user in lower case?

slides.title: Equality, types and string order
slides.say: Read the table row by row and mark the surprise. The decimal sum is a little off, because computers store fractions in binary. Capital Z sorts before small a because of character codes. Ask the class to predict the comparison of two tiny differences.

slides.title: Story: the man inside the bool type
slides.say: George Boole published his algebra of logic in 1847 and 1854, and Python's bool type carries his name. Show the portrait and open the link. Ask the class: where in your own code do you use and, or and not without thinking of him?

slides.title: Chained comparisons: between two limits
slides.say: A chain checks that a value lies between two limits. Python expands it into comparisons joined by and. Example: is fifteen between ten and twenty? Ask the class: how would you write the same test in a language without chains?

slides.title: Chained comparisons
slides.say: Look at the number line on the slide and find the marker for age. The second chain fails at its last link, so the whole chain is False. Ask the class to change age to twenty and predict both answers before the run.

slides.title: Part 2: Boolean operators
slides.say: Part two. The operators and, or and not combine answers. Python stops early and returns an operand, and truthiness lets any value act as true or false. Example: an empty list. Ask the class which values count as false.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: Boolean operators
slides.say: The word and is two locks on one door, or is two doors into one room, and not is a mirror. Example: a club door that checks age and membership. Ask the class which picture is closest to an empty list counting as false.

slides.title: and, or: the truth table
slides.say: The word and needs both sides true, while or needs only one. Example: a door with two locks against a room with two doors. Ask the class: in how many of the four rows is and true, and in how many is or true?

slides.title: and, or: the truth table
slides.say: The table lists all four pairs and the answers of and and or. The chart counts the true results: one for and, three for or. Ask the class to say, in one sentence, when the word or gives False. Change one value in the code, predict the new result, then run it.

slides.title: not, and the order of the operators
slides.say: The word not flips a value, and it binds weaker than the comparison operators. Example: not four equals five is not of the comparison. Ask the class: why do parentheses help a reader even when Python does not need them?

slides.title: not, and the order of the operators
slides.say: Check the order in the table: comparisons, then not, then and, then or. The parentheses in the last line change the answer. Ask the class to add parentheses to the second line so that Python reads it the way a person would.

slides.title: Mixing Boolean and comparison operators
slides.say: A comparison gives a Boolean value, and the Boolean operators join those values. Example: age at least eighteen and a membership. Ask the class: which rule would you write for a cinema ticket with a student discount? Point at the drawing and read its four steps aloud, from left to right.

slides.title: Mixing Boolean and comparison operators
slides.say: Read each row from the left: the comparisons first, then the join, then the result. A member aged twenty-five passes the first test and fails the second. Ask the class to change age to twelve and predict all three answers.

slides.title: Short-circuit: stop early, return an operand
slides.say: The words and and or stop as soon as the answer is known, and they return the operand they stopped at. Example: asking two guards. Ask the class: why is a division by zero safe on the right side of or?

slides.title: and, or: they stop early and return an operand
slides.say: Follow the arrows in the picture to the operand that was returned. The division by zero never runs. Empty text and None count as false. Ask the class to predict what the expression zero and one divided by zero gives, then run it.

slides.title: Truthiness: which values count as false
slides.say: Every value counts as true or false when a condition tests it. Example: an empty shopping bag counts as nothing. Ask the class: why is writing if greeting better than comparing the greeting with True? Let one student retell the four steps in their own words.

slides.title: Truthiness: which values count as false
slides.say: The table shows each value and what bool gives for it. Zero, empty text, an empty list and None are false. A list holding zero is true, because it is not empty. Ask the class which row surprised them most.

slides.title: Part 3: Blocks and branches
slides.say: Part three. A block is a run of indented lines. The statement if runs it on a true condition, and else and elif add the other roads. Watch the order of the rungs. Ask the class what happens when two rungs are true.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: blocks and branches
slides.say: A signpost at a fork sends you one way, a block is a room, and an elif ladder is climbed from the top. Example: a hiking trail with three forks. Ask the class what happens if two rungs are both true.

slides.title: Story: the whitespace that is the syntax
slides.say: Guido van Rossum took the indentation idea from ABC at CWI in Amsterdam, and the design FAQ still defends it. Show the photo and open the link. Ask the class: what could go wrong if the layout and the logic were allowed to disagree?

slides.title: Blocks: lines that belong together
slides.say: A block is the group of lines that belong to one statement, and a colon opens it. Example: the two lines under the senior discount. Ask the class: what would the program print if the age were fifty? Point at the drawing and read its four steps aloud, from left to right.

slides.title: Blocks: the lines that belong to an if
slides.say: Look at the boxes on the slide: the teal ones ran. The two indented lines ran together, and the last line ran in any case. Ask the class to change the age to fifty and say which boxes turn grey.

slides.title: Indentation decides the block
slides.say: In Python the indentation is the syntax, so the layout and the logic can never disagree. Example: a bullet list with a deeper dash. Ask the class: what would happen if the last line were indented as well? Draw the four steps on the board, then compare them with the slide.

slides.title: Indentation decides what belongs to the block
slides.say: The table says which lines ran. The condition is false, so both indented lines were skipped, and only the last line was printed. Ask the class to indent the last line by four spaces, predict the output and then run it.

slides.title: if and else: two roads
slides.say: An if can sit inside the block of another if, and an else belongs to the if at its own indent. Example: first the name, then the password. Ask the class: which message appears for the name Bob? Let one student retell the four steps in their own words.

slides.title: if and else: the password check
slides.say: Follow the teal path through the boxes for this username and password. The inner else is skipped because the password is right. Ask the class to change the password and predict which box lights up instead. Ask a student to read the result picture aloud before you run it.

slides.title: elif: a ladder with one exit
slides.say: An elif is tested only when everything above it was false, so exactly one block runs. Example: a ladder climbed from the top. Ask the class: what is printed for Carol if her age is fifty instead of three thousand?

slides.title: elif: a ladder with one exit
slides.say: The table shows which rungs were tested and which one ran. The first true condition wins and the rest are skipped. Age three thousand stops at the third rung. Ask the class to predict the answer for age eighty. Run the example on the chapter page and compare it with the picture.

slides.title: elif: the order of the rungs
slides.say: A broad test placed too early shadows a narrow test below it. Example: every age above two thousand is also above one hundred. Ask the class: how would you reorder the rungs so that the vampire message can appear? Draw the four steps on the board, then compare them with the slide.

slides.title: elif: the order of the rungs matters
slides.say: Read the results for the four ages. Three thousand is stopped at the grannie rung, so the vampire rung never runs. The chart counts the rungs tested for each age. Ask the class to swap the two rungs and run it again.

slides.title: Part 4: Two short programs
slides.say: Part four. Two short programs from the book use everything so far. Follow the variables line by line, then predict the printed text. Example: Opposite Day flips an answer. Ask the class to say what a trace is.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: two short programs
slides.say: Both programs of the book are small recipes. Opposite Day flips an answer, and the capacity calculator chooses a ratio by unit. A trace is a notebook with one line per step. Ask the class: why does a baker's dozen differ from a dozen?

slides.title: Opposite Day: follow one variable
slides.say: Follow one variable through the lines that ran. On an Opposite Day the flag starts as True, and the answer is then flipped with not. Example: a child who says the opposite. Ask the class: what is printed if the flag is False?

slides.title: A short program: Opposite Day
slides.say: The table is a trace: one row for each line that ran and the value of the variable afterwards. The else lines were skipped. Ask the class to set the flag to False and predict which lines will run. Ask a student to read the result picture aloud before you run it.

slides.title: The Dishonest Capacity Calculator
slides.say: A maker counts a terabyte as ten to the twelve bytes, but a computer counts two to the forty. The ladder picks the ratio by unit. Example: a ten terabyte disk. Ask the class: why does the else keep the program from crashing?

slides.title: A short program: the Dishonest Capacity Calculator
slides.say: The table runs the same code for three units, and the chart sets the advertised size beside the real one. The else gives a ratio of one for an unknown unit. Ask the class to predict the real capacity of a ten gigabyte card.

slides.title: Part 5: Newer Python
slides.say: Part five. Python moved on after the book. The conditional expression, match and the walrus are in current code every day. Example: match replaces a long elif chain. Ask the class which one they would use first.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: newer Python
slides.say: The conditional expression picks one of two values, match sorts by shape, a guard adds a condition and the walrus assigns inside an expression. Example: the post office sorting machine. Ask the class which of the four they would explain to a friend first.

slides.title: The conditional expression
slides.say: The conditional expression picks one of two values in a single line. Example: the word even or the word odd for a number. Ask the class: when is the four-line if and else easier to read than the one-line version?

slides.title: One line: the conditional expression
slides.say: The arrows show which side of the expression was chosen for seven and for ten. In the last line the division by zero is never evaluated. Ask the class to write the same choice with an if and an else and compare the two versions.

slides.title: Story: a thirty-year-old wish, granted in 3.10
slides.say: The match statement arrived in Python 3.10 in October 2021, after PEPs 634 to 636. It is more than a switch, because patterns also bind names. Open the tutorial link. Ask the class: which cases of the next slide could be elif lines?

slides.title: match: a switch that matches patterns
slides.say: The match statement tries the cases from the top and runs the first one that fits. Example: a status code of 403 fits the third case. Ask the class: why must the underscore case stand last? Let one student retell the four steps in their own words.

slides.title: match: a switch that matches patterns
slides.say: The table shows which case caught each status. A pipe joins alternatives into one case. The status 418 falls through to the underscore. Ask the class to add a case for 500 that prints server error, and say where it must stand.

slides.title: match: sequences and captures
slides.say: A pattern can take a list apart and capture a name from it. Example: go north gives the name direction the value north. Ask the class: which of the three commands falls through to the underscore case, and why? Point at the drawing and read its four steps aloud, from left to right.

slides.title: match: sequences and captures
slides.say: The table shows each command and the case that caught it, and the chart counts the items in each list. A list with one item fits the quit case. Ask the class to add a case for a list that starts with take.

slides.title: match: guards
slides.say: A guard adds a condition to a case: the pattern must fit and the guard must be true. Example: a point whose two numbers are equal lies on the diagonal. Ask the class: why must the guarded case stand before the plain case?

slides.title: match: guards
slides.say: The table shows both points and the case that caught each. The point three and three passes the guard, while three and four falls to the plain case. Ask the class to remove the guard and predict what the first case would catch.

slides.title: Story: the walrus that changed who leads Python
slides.say: PEP 572 gave Python the walrus operator in version 3.8, and the debate led Guido van Rossum to step down as BDFL in July 2018. Show the walrus photo. Ask the class: when should a name that is tested also be kept?

slides.title: The walrus: test and keep
slides.say: The walrus operator assigns a value to a name and gives the value back, so one condition can test and keep it. Example: the length of a name. Ask the class: why would you not compute the length twice? Let one student retell the four steps in their own words.

slides.title: The walrus: test and keep in one step
slides.say: The table shows each name, its length and whether the test passed. The name size stays available after the loop and holds the last length. Ask the class to change the limit from three to five and predict which names are printed.

slides.title: Current Python adds more
slides.say: Python moves on, and these features are newer than the book. And and or return operands, match came in 3.10 and the walrus in 3.8. Example: Python 3.14 warns about leaving a finally block. Ask the class which version of Python they have installed.

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: Five sentences to keep. The chart shows how many code examples each part of the chapter has. Example: part five has the most, because Python grew after the book. Ask the class to say the five sentences back in their own words.

slides.title: Practice Questions
slides.say: Four drills. Predict first, then run them on the chapter page. Example: add parentheses to a line so that the order is obvious. Ask each student to explain one answer in a single sentence to the neighbour, then compare the explanations.

slides.title: Resources: where to go next
slides.say: Start with the book chapter, then the Python documentation. The stories link to first-hand sources and the PEPs. Example: PEP 636 is the tutorial for match. Ask the class to choose one link and read it before the next class.
